title: Context
summary: React context shares a value with parts deeper in the page without passing it through every middle part.
introduction: React context shares a value with parts deeper in the page without passing it through every middle part. Imagine a classroom clock that every group can read. Share one useful setting, then learn when normal props are the clearer choice.
learningObjectives: Explain the prop drilling problem that context solves
Create a context, provide a value and read it with useContext or use
Share state and its setter through context
Decide when context is appropriate and when composition is better

blocks.title: Before: the user travels through Layout

blocks.text: `Layout` has no interest in `user`; it only passes it along. With a dozen such components, adding a new shared value means editing all of them, and renaming a prop becomes a project.

`createContext(defaultValue)` creates a context object. Rendering that object as a component with a `value` prop makes the value available to everything inside it. React 19 lets you render the context itself as the provider; in React 18 you had to write `<UserContext.Provider value={user}>`, which still works in 19.

blocks.title: After: context

blocks.text: `useContext(UserContext)` finds the **nearest** `UserContext` provider above the calling component and returns its value. If there is none, it returns the default passed to `createContext`, here `null`. Providers can nest: an inner provider overrides the outer one for its own subtree, which is how you give one section of a page a different theme.
React 19 adds `use`, which reads a context like `useContext` but may be called inside conditions and loops. This is handy when a component only needs the value in some branches.

With a SettingsContext value of { currency: 'EUR' }

blocks.text: A context value is just a value, so it can be an object holding state **and** the function to change it. Put the `useState` call in a provider component and expose both.

blocks.title: ThemeContext.jsx
App.jsx
Rendered
blocks.content:
initially:        <main class="light"><button>Theme: light</button></main>
after one click:  <main class="dark"><button>Theme: dark</button></main>

blocks.text: Exporting a `useTheme` hook next to the provider keeps the context object private and gives consumers one obvious import. When a value is required, create the context with `undefined` as the default and make the hook throw a clear error if it finds it, instead of letting `undefined.theme` crash somewhere far away:

Every component that reads a context re-renders when the provider's `value` changes, compared with `Object.is`. `value={{ theme, toggle }}` creates a new object on every render of the provider, so all consumers re-render whenever the provider renders, even if `theme` did not change. For small apps that is fine. When it becomes a problem, memoize the object with `useMemo`, split rarely-changing and frequently-changing values into separate contexts, or let the [React Compiler](/tutorials/react/performance-memo) do the memoization.

blocks.title: Common mistake: forgetting the provider
blocks.text: Reading a context with no provider above does not throw; it silently returns the default value from `createContext`. If that default is `null` you get `Cannot read properties of null` somewhere unrelated, and if it is a placeholder object the UI looks wrong without any error. Wrap the tree in the provider in `main.jsx` or `App.jsx`, and make your custom hook fail loudly when the provider is missing.

items: **Passing data two levels down.** Props are simpler and easier to trace.
**Avoiding a prop you could compose away.** Often the intermediate component can accept `children` and the parent can render the consumer directly, which removes the drilling without context.
**High-frequency updates** such as the mouse position or a text input's value: every consumer re-renders on each change. Keep that state local or in a dedicated store.
**Server data.** Fetching and caching is better handled by a library such as TanStack Query, covered in [Fetching and Caching Data](/tutorials/react/data-fetching).

blocks.text: Good uses: theme, locale, the authenticated user, a form's shared state, and dependency injection such as an API client.

questions.question: Which React 19 syntax provides a context value to a subtree?
questions.explanation: In React 19 the context object itself can be rendered as the provider with a `value` prop. `<ThemeContext.Provider>` still works; the other options do not exist.

questions.question: A component that calls `useContext` re-renders whenever the nearest provider's value changes.
questions.explanation: That is how context propagates updates. It is also why a new object literal in `value` on every render re-renders every consumer.

seo.title: React Context – Share Data Without Prop Drilling
seo.description: Learn React context: createContext, the React 19 provider syntax, reading values with useContext and use, sharing state via a provider and when to avoid it.
